exercises.objective: Explain how the Bellman residual generalizes Q-learning's single-sample TD update.
exercises.prompt: Explain why RL-03's Q-learning TD update, $\alpha[r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')-Q(s,a)]$, is 'a gradient step on the loss $\tfrac12[r+\gamma Q(s',\pi(s'))-Q(s,a)]^2$,' and why storing a whole replay buffer instead of one transition changes this from a table update into a genuine ML training problem.
hints: Differentiating $\tfrac12[r+\gamma Q(s',\pi(s'))-Q(s,a)]^2$ w.r.t. a tabular $Q(s,a)$ entry (treating everything else as fixed) gives exactly $-[r+\gamma Q(s',\pi(s'))-Q(s,a)]$; a gradient-descent step of size $\alpha$ on this loss is exactly Q-learning's update.

For a single tabular entry, 'the loss' and 'the TD error' are the same computation viewed two ways. But once $Q$ is a neural network $Q_\theta(s,a)$ instead of a table, you can't update one entry in isolation, you need a genuine loss function summed over data to compute a gradient w.r.t. all of $\theta$ at once.

The Bellman residual $B_\mathcal{D}^\pi=\sum_{(s,a,r,s')\in\mathcal{D}}[r+\gamma\bar Q(s',\pi(s'))-Q(s,a)]^2$ is exactly this: sum the per-transition squared TD error over the whole replay buffer, making it an ordinary supervised regression loss (ML-02/ML-04) that SGD (OPT-05) can train $\theta$ against directly.

exercises.objective: Derive the log-derivative trick identity used in the policy gradient theorem.
exercises.prompt: Starting from the ordinary chain rule applied to $\log P_\theta(\xi)$, derive $\dfrac{\partial P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta} = P_\theta(\xi)\dfrac{\partial\log P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta}$.
hints: By the chain rule (ML-01), $\dfrac{\partial\log P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta} = \dfrac{1}{P_\theta(\xi)}\dfrac{\partial P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta}$ (the derivative of $\log$ is $1/(\cdot)$, times the inner derivative).

$P_\theta(\xi)\dfrac{\partial\log P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta} = \dfrac{\partial P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta}$: exactly the identity used to rewrite $\partial J/\partial\theta$ as an expectation under $P_\theta$. (Independently verified symbolically with SymPy for a concrete example distribution while authoring this module.)

exercises.objective: Derive that the trajectory log-probability's theta-gradient reduces to a sum of policy log-probability gradients.
exercises.prompt: Given $P_\theta(\xi)=P(s_0)\prod_t\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)$, derive $\dfrac{\partial\log P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta}=\sum_t\dfrac{\partial\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\partial\theta}$, and explain why the environment's dynamics $P(s'\mid s,a)$ don't appear.
hints: Taking $\log$ of a product turns it into a sum: $\log P_\theta(\xi)=\log P(s_0)+\sum_t\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)+\sum_t\log P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)$.

Differentiate term by term w.r.t. $\theta$: $P(s_0)$ and $P(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t)$ are properties of the environment, not the policy, so they don't depend on $\theta$ at all, and their derivatives are exactly zero.

Only the $\sum_t\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)$ terms depend on $\theta$, giving $\dfrac{\partial\log P_\theta(\xi)}{\partial\theta}=\sum_t\dfrac{\partial\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\partial\theta}$: the environment's dynamics never appear in the gradient because they were never a function of $\theta$ in the first place, only the policy $\pi_\theta$ is.

exercises.objective: Explain why a delayed target network stabilizes Bellman residual training.
exercises.prompt: Explain what specifically goes wrong if you train $Q_\theta$ against a target that also uses the current, live $Q_\theta$ (i.e. $\bar Q\equiv Q_\theta$), and how a delayed/low-pass-filtered $\bar Q$ fixes it.
hints: If the target $r+\gamma\bar Q(s',\pi(s'))$ uses the same live $Q_\theta$ being trained, every gradient step that changes $\theta$ also immediately changes the target the next step is trying to match: the thing you're chasing moves every time you take a step toward it.

This 'moving target' feedback loop can oscillate or diverge, since the loss landscape itself is shifting as $\theta$ updates, unlike ordinary supervised regression where the targets $y_i$ are fixed constants.

Freezing $\bar Q$ to a delayed/low-pass-filtered copy of $\theta$ (updated only occasionally, or slowly averaged) breaks this feedback loop: for many consecutive gradient steps, the target is effectively constant, turning training back into an ordinary, well-behaved regression problem, at the cost of the target lagging slightly behind the true current $Q_\theta$.
